Black Square. Kazimir Malevich's 1915 painting is an austere work depicting a pure black square on a white background, representing the ultimate reduction of painting to essential form and Malevich's vision of what he called the zero of form. This radical work inaugurates Suprematism and remains one of the most philosophically charged minimalist artworks, asserting that non-representational abstraction can contain spiritual meaning.

Exhibited in 1915 at the Last Futurist Exhibition in Petrograd, Malevich intended it as the endpoint of representation and the zero from which new art would emerge. The canvas is simple: a black square on white, executed with visible brushwork that emphasizes the painter's gesture even while pursuing absolute abstraction. Malevich theorized the work as beyond mere form, as a spiritual icon expressing pure feeling and cosmic consciousness, comparable to religious icons in Russian tradition. He declared it the end of painting as representation and the birth of art based on pure sensation and abstraction, an extreme position even among the Russian avant-garde.

Malevich created multiple versions of Black Square, including one painted between 1920 and 1930 and now held at the State Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow, indicating his obsession with the theme. The work has influenced every major movement in abstract and conceptual art since, from Minimalism to Conceptualism, and the square itself became a foundational unit of visual language.
